notes.meaning: As Jesus and His disciples walked through the fields on the Sabbath, the disciples picked and ate grain because they were hungry. God's law allowed travelers to pluck grain by hand from a neighbor's field to satisfy immediate hunger. The disciples were not stealing, but simply gathering food to eat as they walked.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many careful students of the old manuscripts think the words 'second-first' were added later by copyists. They are missing from several important manuscripts, which is why many modern Bibles simply say 'one Sabbath.'

notes.meaning: The Pharisees questioned the disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath day of rest. These religious leaders did not accuse them of stealing, but of doing forbidden work on a holy day. Under their human traditions, plucking and rubbing the grain was treated like reaping and threshing in the harvest.

Jesus answered the critics by pointing back to an event from Scripture involving King David. When David and his men were hungry and on the run, the priest gave them sacred bread from the tabernacle that only priests were normally allowed to eat. Jesus showed that meeting urgent human need matters more to God than keeping ceremonial rules.

Jesus announced that as the Son of Man, He is Lord over the Sabbath day. Since He gave the Sabbath to mankind in the first place, He has the authority to interpret its true purpose. The day of rest was designed to bless human beings rather than lay heavy burdens upon them.

differ.view: The moral duty of the fourth commandment remains, shifting the Sabbath rest to the first day of the week as the Lord's Day.
Christ is the believer's true rest, meaning the Old Testament weekly Sabbath command is fulfilled and no longer legally binding.

notes.meaning: On another Sabbath, Jesus entered the local synagogue and began teaching the people. While He taught, a man was present whose right hand was withered and paralyzed. The loss of his right hand made it very hard for the man to work and earn a living.

The scribes and Pharisees watched Jesus intently to see if He would heal the man on the Sabbath. Rabbinic tradition allowed medical care on the Sabbath only if a person's life was in immediate danger. Because this man was not dying, the leaders hoped to use a healing to bring formal charges against Jesus.

Jesus knew the hostile thoughts and schemes of the religious leaders before they uttered a word. Instead of avoiding a confrontation, He told the man with the withered hand to stand in front of the whole gathering. By bringing the man into the center, Jesus prepared to address the issue openly.

Jesus asked the religious leaders whether the Sabbath law was meant for doing good or doing evil, for saving life or destroying it. He showed that neglecting to help someone when you have the power to do so is the same as doing harm. While Jesus intended to heal and preserve life, His opponents were using the holy day to plot His death.

Jesus looked around at the entire room and commanded the man to stretch out his paralyzed hand. The man trusted Jesus and reached out, and his hand was instantly restored to full health. Jesus performed this great miracle with a word alone, exposing the leaders' lack of compassion.

The scribes and Pharisees were overcome with irrational fury when they saw the man healed. They were humiliated because Jesus had exposed their hard hearts and left them unable to answer. Out of deep resentment, they began plotting among themselves what they might do to stop Him.

Jesus went out to a mountain alone and spent the whole night in prayer to God. He regularly withdrew from the crowds to pray, especially before major steps in His ministry. This long night of devotion prepared Him to choose the men who would lead His church.

When morning arrived, Jesus summoned His larger group of followers and chose twelve of them for a special role. He called them apostles, a word that means messengers sent out with personal authority to represent Him. The twelve leaders pointed to the twelve tribes of Israel, showing that God was renewing His people.

Luke records the names of the twelve apostles to identify the core group Jesus selected. The list includes ordinary fishermen like Peter, Andrew, James, and John, alongside Matthew, a former tax collector for Rome, and Simon the Zealot, who had opposed Roman rule. It ends with Judas Iscariot, who later betrayed the Lord, showing how diverse and fragile this chosen group would be.

Jesus walked down the mountain with His newly chosen apostles and stopped on a level area. A large group of His followers met Him there, joined by a vast crowd from across Judea, Jerusalem, and the northern seacoast cities of Tyre and Sidon. The crowds came from far and wide eager to hear His teaching and receive healing.

The people came seeking cures for all kinds of physical sicknesses and relief from spiritual torment. Jesus showed His complete authority by restoring their health and setting free those afflicted by unclean spirits. No form of human suffering was beyond His mercy or His power.

The entire crowd pressed forward, desperate just to touch Jesus as He stood among them. Healing power poured out from Him like a living fountain, curing every person who reached out. His compassion reached everyone without turning a single needy person away.

Jesus looked directly at His disciples and declared that the poor are blessed because the kingdom of God belongs to them. In the Bible, being blessed means having God's favor and true spiritual joy. Those who have little in this world and depend fully on God receive the lasting treasures of His kingdom.

differ.view: Jesus mainly means poverty of spirit, as Matthew words it: people who know they have nothing to offer and depend on God.

notes.meaning: Jesus promised that those who suffer hunger now will be fully satisfied, and those who weep now will laugh. He spoke to people enduring real physical need and deep spiritual longing for God's righteousness. God will one day wipe away the sorrows of His faithful people and replace them with everlasting joy.

Jesus told His followers that they are blessed even when people hate, insult, and reject them on His account. In that society, this meant being cast out of the synagogue, cutting believers off from community worship and daily social life. Experiencing mistreatment for following Christ is a badge of true loyalty to Him.

Jesus commanded His followers to leap for joy when they are persecuted, because a great reward awaits them in heaven. God's ancient prophets faced the exact same suffering and rejection from earlier generations for delivering His word. Disciples who endure mistreatment can know they stand in holy company.

Jesus pronounced a solemn warning of sorrow over those who are rich and satisfied in this present life. People who trust in earthly wealth and comfort have already received all the satisfaction they will ever get. Placing ultimate security in worldly possessions leaves the heart unprepared for eternity.
